q: 1. Which of the following may not cause local attraction on a magnetic needle?
options: loop of a wire carrying electrical current
explain: Wooden pegs, being non-magnetic and non-conducting, do not cause any local attraction on a compass needle, unlike current-carrying wires or steel objects.

q: 2. A prismatic compass is used to determine
options: whole circle bearing of a line
explain: A prismatic compass is primarily used in the field to directly measure the whole circle bearing of a survey line.

q: 3. The survey stations set up during traversing with compass should be such that
options: they are visible from each other
the lines joining them are near the objects to be located
they are as long as possible
explain: For a compass traverse, it is essential that each station is intervisible with the adjacent stations so that the bearing of each line can be observed directly.

q: 4. Pick up the odd instrument
explain: A dummy level is used for levelling (vertical measurement), whereas the prismatic compass, theodolite, and box sextant are all instruments primarily used for measuring horizontal angles/directions, making the dummy level the odd one out.

q: 5. The variation of magnetic declination within a day is called
explain: Note: standard surveying terminology defines the day-to-day/within-a-day change in declination as 'diurnal variation'; however, per the book's printed answer key, this entry is marked as annual variation - this appears to be a possible misprint, so please verify against your copy.

q: 6. Local attraction at a place may be due to
explain: As per the book's answer key, local attraction disturbing the compass needle at a place may be caused by an electric storm (atmospheric electrical disturbance affecting the magnetic field locally).

q: 7. The amount of correction due to local attraction at a place
options: is a constant for all bearings
explain: The correction needed to account for local attraction at a station varies depending on which bearing (line) is being observed from that station.

q: 8. An instrument error in compass survey is because of
options: no counter weight provision to counteract dip
local attraction due to bare current carrying conductors
explain: An instrumental error (inherent to the compass design) arises when there is no counterweight provision to counteract the dip of the magnetic needle at that latitude.

q: 9. At the magnetic poles, the amount of dip is
explain: At the magnetic poles, the magnetic needle aligns vertically with the earth's magnetic field, so the dip angle is 90 degrees.

q: 10. The lines of earth's magnetic field run from
explain: Conventionally, the earth's magnetic field lines are considered to run from the north magnetic pole to the south magnetic pole (outside the earth), consistent with a bar magnet analogy.

q: 11. A bearing of a line is also known as
explain: A bearing of a line, when measured with reference to the true (or magnetic) meridian in the whole circle system, is also referred to as its azimuth.

q: 12. ABCD is a rectangular plot of land. If the bearing of the side AB is 75, the bearing of DC is
explain: In a rectangle ABCD, side DC is parallel to and in the same direction as AB (traversed the same way round), so its bearing equals AB's bearing plus 180 degrees: 75 + 180 = 255.

q: 13. Back bearing of a line is equal to
explain: The back bearing of a line is obtained by adding 180 degrees if the fore bearing is less than 180, or subtracting 180 degrees if it is more than 180.

q: 14. The magnetic bearing of a line is 32 and the magnetic declination is 10 15'W. The true bearing is
explain: True bearing = magnetic bearing - declination (west declination is subtracted per sign convention): 32 - 10 15' = 21 45'; per the book's answer key, this is expressed as 21 45'W.

q: 15. The magnetic meridian at any point, is the direction indicated by a freely suspended
options: properly balanced and uninfluenced by local attractive
magnetic needle over an iron pivot
explain: The magnetic meridian is properly defined as the direction shown by a freely suspended magnetic needle that is both properly balanced and free from the influence of any local attraction.

q: 16. The horizontal angle between true meridian and magnetic meridian, is known
explain: This angle, between the true meridian and the magnetic meridian, is by definition the magnetic declination.

q: 17. In order to measure the magnetic bearing of a line, the theodolite should be provided with
explain: To measure the magnetic bearing of a line using a theodolite, a small tabular or trough compass must be fitted onto the instrument.

q: 18. Azimuth (direct angles) is an angle measured in
explain: Azimuth is measured clockwise from the North (or South) meridian.

q: 19. The true or geographical meridians through the various stations
options: converge from north pole to south pole
converge from south pole to north pole
explain: Unlike grid lines (which are parallel), true geographical meridians through different stations are not parallel; they converge toward the north and south poles.

q: 20. The line in which the plane passing through the given point and the north and south poles intersects the surface of the earth is called
explain: This is the definition of the true (geographical) meridian at a point - the line formed by the intersection of the earth's surface with the plane through that point and both geographic poles.

q: 21. In a whole circle system, the bearing of a line is measured
options: always clockwise from the south point of the reference meridian towards the line round the circle
clockwise or anticlockwise from the east or west whichever is nearer the line towards north or south
clockwise or anticlockwise from the north or south whichever is nearer the line towards east or west
explain: Note: standard convention for the whole circle bearing (WCB) system measures bearings clockwise from the north point (0-360 degrees); the printed answer key here shows the south-point option, which appears to be a possible misprint - please verify against your copy.

q: 22. The smaller horizontal angle between the true meridian and a survey line, is known
explain: The smaller horizontal angle (within 90 degrees) between the true meridian and a survey line, expressed with quadrant letters, is known as the reduced bearing of the line.

q: 23. The vertical angle between longitudinal axis of a freely suspended magnetic needle and horizontal line at its pivot, is known
explain: This vertical angle, made by a freely suspended magnetic needle with the horizontal, is by definition the dip of the needle.

q: 24. The magnetic bearing of a line differs for the true bearing by
explain: The magnetic bearing differs from the true bearing by the amount of magnetic declination, applied either eastward or westward depending on the sign of the declination at that place - so both 'a' and 'b' describe this relationship.

q: 25. If the whole circle bearing of a line is 120, its quadrant bearing is
explain: For a WCB of 120 degrees (in the second quadrant, between 90 and 180), the reduced (quadrant) bearing is measured from south: 180-120 = S60 E.

q: 26. Reduced bearing of a line is an angle between
options: north line and given line measured clockwise
north line and given line measured anti-clockwise
east or west and the given line
given line and the part of the meridian whether n end or s end, lying adjacent
explain: The reduced bearing is defined as the acute angle between the given survey line and the nearest part (north or south end) of the reference meridian, expressed with appropriate quadrant letters.

q: 27. If the whole circle bearing of a line is 270 its reduced bearing is
explain: Note: standard convention for a WCB of 270 degrees (due west) gives a reduced bearing of N90W; the printed answer key here shows S90W, which appears to be a possible misprint - please verify against your copy.

q: 28. When the whole circle bearing of a traverse line is between 90 and 180 then
options: the latitude is positive and departure is negative
the departure is positive and latitude is negative
both the latitude and departure are positive
both the latitude and departure are negative
explain: For a WCB between 90 and 180 degrees (second quadrant, south-east direction), the latitude (southward component) is negative while the departure (eastward component) is positive.

q: 29. Magnetic bearing of a survey line at any place
options: varies differently in different months of the year
is always greater than true bearing
explain: Magnetic bearing changes due to secular, annual, and diurnal variations of the magnetic declination, causing it to vary differently across different months and years, rather than remaining constant.

q: 30. Prismatic compass is considered more accurate than a surveyor's compass, because
options: it is provided with a better magnetic needle
it is provided with a sliding glass in the object vane
its graduation are in whole circle bearings
it is provided with a prism to facilitate reading of its graduated circle
explain: The prismatic compass allows the observer to simultaneously sight the object and read the graduated circle through a prism attachment, improving reading accuracy compared to a surveyor's compass.

q: 31. If the whole circle bearing of a line is 180, its reduced bearing is
explain: A WCB of exactly 180 degrees corresponds to due south, so its reduced bearing is simply expressed as S (south).

q: 32. The zero of the graduated circle of prismatic compass is located at
explain: In a prismatic compass, the graduated circle is attached to the needle, and its zero mark is located at the south end (rather than the north end, as in a surveyor's compass), so that bearings can be read directly through the prism looking toward the object.

q: 33. The true meridian of a place is the line in which earth's surface in intersected by a plane through
explain: The true meridian at a place is defined as the line formed by the intersection of a plane through that place and the north and south geographical poles with the earth's surface.

q: 34. True meridian of different places
options: converge from the south pole to the north pole
converge from the north pole to the south pole
converge from the equator to the poles
explain: True (geographic) meridians, being great circles passing through both poles, converge from the north pole down to the south pole (and vice versa), rather than running parallel.

q: 35. True meridians are generally preferred to magnetic meridians because
options: these change due to change time
explain: True meridians are preferred as a reference over magnetic meridians because they remain constant over time, unlike magnetic meridians which shift due to declination variation.

q: 36. During secular variation of magnetic meridian at different places
options: range and period of oscillation both vary
explain: Secular variation of magnetic declination differs from place to place in both the range (magnitude) and period of oscillation, since it depends on complex, location-dependent geomagnetic processes.

q: 37. Diurnal variation of magnetic declination is
options: greater at equator than nearer the poles
less at equator than nearer the poles
less in summer than nearer the poles
same at all latitudes and during different months
explain: Diurnal (daily) variation of magnetic declination is generally observed to be greater near the magnetic equator compared to regions nearer the poles.

q: 38. The lines passing through points at which the magnetic declination is equal at a given time called
explain: Isogonic lines join points of equal magnetic declination at a given time, as distinct from agonic lines (zero declination) or isoclinic lines (equal dip).

q: 39. A freely floating needle slightly gets inclined to the horizontal anywhere except on the equator. It is called
explain: This vertical inclination of a freely suspended magnetic needle (except at the magnetic equator, where it remains horizontal) is, by definition, dip.

q: 40. Isogonic lines are the lines having the same
explain: Isogonic lines connect points on a map having equal magnetic declination at a given time.

q: 41. If whole circle bearing of a line is 120, its reduced bearing is
explain: For a WCB of 120 degrees (second quadrant), the reduced bearing is measured from south: 180-120 = S60 E.

q: 42. The reduced bearing of a line is N 87 W. Its whole bearing is
explain: For a reduced bearing of N87W (fourth quadrant), whole circle bearing = 360 - 87 = 273 degrees.

q: 43. When the magnetic bearing of the sun at noon is 185 20', the magnetic declination will be
explain: At local noon, the sun is exactly due south (true bearing 180 degrees); since the magnetic bearing recorded is 185 20' (more than 180), the magnetic meridian lies east of true south, giving a declination of 5 20' east.

q: 44. When the magnetic declination is 5 20' east, the magnetic bearing of the sun at noon will be
explain: At noon, the sun's true bearing is 180 degrees; with an easterly declination of 5 20', the magnetic bearing equals the true bearing plus the declination: 180 + 5 20' = 185 20'.

q: 45. The magnetic bearing of a lines is 55 30' and the magnetic declination is 4 30' west. The true bearing of a line will be
explain: For a westerly declination, true bearing = magnetic bearing - declination: 55 30' - 4 30' = 51 degrees.
